claims.text: The noble-metal ions in the starting salt mixture have intrinsically different redox potentials.
Changing pH or adding selected chemicals can bring the effective reduction potentials of the different metal ions into close alignment.
Alignment of effective reduction potentials causes the different metal ions to reduce nearly simultaneously.
Nearly simultaneous reduction produces synchronized nucleation of the constituent metals.
Synchronized nucleation drives one-step formation of uniformly alloyed nanoparticles.
Synchronized reduction and nucleation are the key determinant of homogeneous noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticle formation.
Aligning the effective reduction potentials suppresses sequential and competitive nanoparticle-formation dynamics.
Sequential or competitive formation dynamics lead to phase separation or elemental segregation.
The environmentally adjusted reaction will produce more single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticles than the unchanged baseline.
The environmentally adjusted reaction will produce more compositionally homogeneous nanoparticles than the unchanged baseline.
Nanoparticles produced under the adjusted environment will retain abundant surface atoms for catalysis.
Under unadjusted conditions, differences in reduction kinetics cause phase inhomogeneity and elemental segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies to multimetal noble-metal systems whose constituents have substantially different reduction potentials.
The proposed mechanism may not govern systems in which strong ligand coordination dominates nucleation and growth.
The proposed mechanism may not govern systems in which heterogeneous nucleation on supports dominates nucleation and growth.
Minor differences among the constituent-metal reduction kinetics may persist after environmental adjustment.
Residues from the additives may adversely affect surface catalytic properties.
